newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Row stalls privatisation of Ukraine oil refinery.
newsitem.headline: Row stalls privatisation of Ukraine oil refinery.

text.p: A legal dispute between Ukraine's president and parliament has stalled privatisation of the former Soviet republic's second largest oil refinery, a presidential spokesman said on Wednesday.

Leonid Pidpalov, deputy head of President Leonid Kuchma's administration, told reporters Kuchma had vetoed a law passed by deputies last month which foresaw a tender selling the right to manage the state's stake in Lisichansknaftoorgsyntez (LINOS).

Fearing foreign investment in its six refineries -- especially from Russia which supplies almost all of Ukraine's oil -- the deputies said the tender to manage the 75.3 percent government stake would only be open to Ukrainian-based firms with no more than 25 percent foreign capital.
The management contract is seen as a first step towards a selloff of part of the refinery.
Ukrainian officials have said that Russia has been pressing for some time for a 40-45 per cent stake in LINOS, and this has been one of the issues at Russian-Ukrainian talks.
But in defending the veto on Wednesday, Pidpalov skirted the issue of the nationality of the tender contestants and said the veto should not bring a confrontation with parliament.
"The presidential veto was inspired solely by legal reasons," Pidpalov said.
Ukrainian media have warned against Russian participation in the deal. They said TNK RUNO was the main contender for the stake and was not among leading players on Russia's oil market.

"Such an undertaking is not only unprofitable for the country but also is dangerous for its energy sector," the daily Den wrote recently. "The veto could be viewed (in Ukraine) as moving control of Ukraine's oil market into Moscow's hands."
Pidpalov's criticism centered on parliamentary domination of a special 19-member commission envisaged in the law holding the tender and looking after privatisation of LINOS.
The law stated that 14 members should be deputies and the rest government, State Property Fund and LINOS representatives.
"This law did not obey the Constitution which foresaw the government and not parliament having the right to deal with state property," he said.

Representatives of Ukraine's leading oil company, Ukreximnaftoproduct, seen as the main contender for the 75.3 stake following parliament's passage of the law, declined to comment on the presidential veto.
But LINOS director Vyacheslav Lobach welcomed Kuchma's decision on Wednesday.

"Why should deputies run the plant?" Lobach said by telephone from Lisichansk, some 700 km (440 miles) east of the capital Kiev. He added Russian investors were best because all oil refined at Lisichansk comes from Russia.
"By the time Ukraine finds non-Russian oil sources, the plant will be scrap metal," Lobach said. "We are inextricably tied to Russia."

LINOS owes $100 million to West Deutsche Landesbank AG, which allocated a credit in 1993 with guarantees from the Ukrainian government. The plant also owes about 136 million hryvnias ($75.5 million) to domestic firms. A court case considering LINOS' bankruptcy is now more than a year old.

Investor conditions under the now-vetoed parliamentary law and also accepted by LINOS management, were to pay off all debts and guarantee oil supplies of at least six million tonnes yearly for seven years.
Under Ukrainian law, parliament can ask Kuchma to cancel his veto. If he refuses the constitutional court must decide.
Last year LINOS refined 2.15 million tonnes of oil, compared to 21.8 million tonnes in 1990.
Lobach said LINOS was due to refine 3.5 million tonnes this year. Ukraine's six refineries are capable of refining 60 million tonnes annually but produce far less than that.
